item.title: Free AI property portal launches claiming more listings than Rightmove
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

A new property portal named MyPorta has launched in the UK with an artificial intelligence-powered platform and a bold claim – it currently lists over 182,000 more available properties than Rightmove. The free-to-list service for agents reports 860,242 active UK listings compared to Rightmove's 678,002, representing a 26.9% lead in inventory volume according to September 2023 figures.

How MyPorta gathers its listings

Unlike conventional property portals that rely on agents manually uploading listings or providing data feeds, MyPorta automatically indexes properties advertised on estate and letting agents' public websites. Each listing remains attributed to the original agent, with potential buyers and renters directed back to the agent's own website to enquire. Agents can also choose to upload properties directly or connect their existing CRM systems.

The company emphasises its no-cost proposition for agents, removing what it describes as a historic barrier in the portal market. MyPorta CEO Mal McCallion states: "Estate agents were told they could never leave the old portal model because of inventory. That argument has just disappeared." The platform's automated aggregation approach appears particularly effective in Scotland and Northern Ireland, where its claimed lead over Rightmove's available listings is most pronounced.

Regional listing comparisons

MyPorta's data suggests significant regional variations in inventory coverage compared to Rightmove:

  • London: 165,732 properties listed vs Rightmove's 86,780
  • England (excluding London): 597,391 vs 542,556
  • Scotland: 52,359 vs 20,063
  • Wales: 29,860 vs 28,500
  • Northern Ireland: 14,900 vs 103

These figures exclude properties marked as sold subject to contract, under offer or let agreed. MyPorta sourced Rightmove's public data through sitemaps before applying deduplication and geographical checks. The company acknowledges Rightmove maintains a larger total inventory when including properties in these excluded statuses.

AI-powered property search

Beyond inventory volume, MyPorta aims to differentiate itself through AI-enhanced search functionality. Rather than relying solely on traditional filters, the platform allows users to describe their ideal property in natural language. This artificial intelligence approach may appeal to buyers and renters who find conventional search tools restrictive or time-consuming.

For estate agents, the emergence of a free listing alternative could present new considerations when allocating marketing budgets. While Rightmove and Zoopla maintain strong brand recognition, cost-conscious agents might explore supplementing their portal presence with this new AI-driven option. Property seekers, meanwhile, gain access to an additional channel that claims to aggregate more available listings than the market leader.

item.title: Property portal model ‘on its last legs’ as Rightmove takeover talk grows
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The traditional property portal model could be facing a significant shake-up, according to industry experts, as speculation grows around a potential takeover of Rightmove. Trevor Abrahmsohn, managing director of Glentree Estates and founder of OnTheMarket, has described the current portal model as "on its last legs", arguing that artificial intelligence (AI) is poised to revolutionise how consumers search for properties. His remarks come at a time when Rightmove finds itself under the spotlight, with US activist investor Sachem Head reportedly acquiring a 6% stake in the company.

The Rise of AI in Property Search

Abrahmsohn believes that AI will fundamentally alter the way buyers and sellers interact with property listings. Traditional portals, he argues, may soon become less relevant as AI-driven tools enable consumers to find homes without relying on conventional search methods. This shift could disrupt the longstanding relationships between portals and estate agents, potentially challenging the dominance of established players like Rightmove.

Drawing parallels with technological disruptions that impacted companies such as Kodak and Polaroid, Abrahmsohn suggests that the property portal model could face a similar fate. He predicts that AI will "engulf" the traditional approach, forcing portals to adapt or risk becoming obsolete. Rightmove, however, is already investing heavily in AI and technology, aiming to enhance its role in the home-moving process and stay ahead of emerging competition.

Rightmove’s Future Under Scrutiny

The speculation around Rightmove’s future has intensified following Sachem Head’s significant investment. The activist investor reportedly views Rightmove’s shares as undervalued, believing that the market has overreacted to the potential threat posed by AI. Sachem Head has encouraged Rightmove to utilise debt to finance further share buybacks, a move that could bolster its share price in the short term.

Rightmove’s shares have experienced notable volatility in recent years, peaking at £8.18 in summer 2025 before dropping to £4.10 in May this year. They have since stabilised at around £5. Abrahmsohn questions whether Sachem Head will remain a long-term shareholder, speculating that the investor may look to exit its position after benefiting from a recovery in the share price.

The Broader Impact on Estate Agents

For estate agents, these developments come amidst ongoing debates about portal fees, competition, and the future of online property search. Rightmove continues to dominate the UK market, but the emergence of AI-powered tools is increasing pressure on the traditional listings model. Agents may need to reassess their reliance on portals and explore alternative methods to connect with buyers and sellers.

As the property market evolves, homeowners and industry professionals alike may wish to stay informed about these changes. While Rightmove’s position remains strong for now, the growing influence of AI and the involvement of activist investors could signal a new chapter for property portals in the UK.

The coming months are likely to bring further developments, as Rightmove and its competitors navigate the challenges and opportunities presented by technological advancements. For those involved in the property market, keeping a close eye on these trends could prove essential in adapting to a rapidly changing landscape.

item.title: The landlord register is coming: Agents need to decide now what role they will play
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

The introduction of a national landlord register in England marks a significant shift for the private rental sector. Set to launch in the West Midlands on 15 December 2026, the "Register your rental property" service will be rolled out region by region, with full implementation expected by November 2027. Landlords will be required to pay an annual fee of £65 per property and will have three months to comply once registration becomes mandatory in their area. This new system aims to bring greater transparency and accountability to the rental market whilst helping tenants make informed decisions.

What does the landlord register mean for the rental sector?

The landlord register is designed to create a comprehensive database of rental properties across England. For tenants, it offers a clearer picture of the properties they are considering, ensuring landlords meet their legal obligations. Responsible landlords may also benefit, as the register provides a platform to demonstrate compliance with regulations. Additionally, local authorities could use the data to target resources more effectively, focusing on properties or landlords that pose the highest risk.

However, the success of the register will largely depend on its implementation. Whilst the initiative is a positive step towards improving standards in the private rental sector, there are potential challenges. Regional rollout timelines, for instance, could create confusion, particularly for landlords with properties in multiple areas. Portfolio landlords, in particular, will need to navigate different deadlines based on the location of each property.

What role will letting agents play?

Although the legal responsibility for registration lies with landlords, letting agents may still face practical and commercial considerations. Agents could find themselves at risk of disputes over the services they provide or the fees they charge in relation to registration. As such, it could be worth agents clarifying their role in the process early on, ensuring both landlords and tenants understand their responsibilities.

For larger portfolio landlords, registering all properties at once from December 2026 may prove simpler than adhering to staggered regional deadlines. Letting agents will need to stay informed about the rollout schedule and advise their clients accordingly. Clear communication and proactive planning could help avoid misunderstandings and ensure compliance is managed smoothly.

The introduction of the landlord register is a welcome development for the rental sector, promising greater transparency and accountability. Whilst challenges remain, effective implementation could benefit tenants, landlords, and local authorities alike. Letting agents, in particular, have an opportunity to play a pivotal role in supporting landlords through this transition.

item.title: AI-generated buyer complaints are slowing property transactions, conveyancers warn
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

Conveyancers are warning that the growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) by homebuyers could lead to delays in property transactions. Reports suggest that buyers are increasingly turning to AI tools to draft complaints, generate extensive queries, and set deadlines, creating additional work for legal professionals. Whilst technology can be helpful, experts argue that AI often lacks the full context of a transaction, potentially complicating the conveyancing process.

The impact of AI-generated queries

Buyers are using AI to compile detailed lists of questions covering a wide range of topics, from service charges and planned works to lease terms and fire safety. Whilst these queries are understandable, the issue arises when AI generates demands based on incomplete or inaccurate information. For instance, buyers may raise issues that have already been addressed or request details that are not yet available from the seller’s solicitor.

Leasehold transactions, which often involve multiple third parties, could be particularly affected by this trend. Estate agents and conveyancers are finding that AI-generated correspondence adds another layer of complexity to sales progression, potentially slowing down the process.

Why AI can complicate conveyancing

One of the key challenges with AI tools is their inability to understand the full history of a transaction or identify which party is responsible for providing specific information. As a result, AI-generated responses may sound authoritative but are often based on assumptions or generalised data. This can lead to misunderstandings and unnecessary delays.

For example, in one case cited by RG Law, a buyer submitted a detailed list of questions about fire safety, asbestos, service charges, and lease terms. Whilst some of these points had already been addressed in reports sent to the client, other information was still outstanding from the seller’s solicitor. The use of AI in this instance created additional work for the conveyancer, delaying the transaction further.

The broader context of conveyancing complaints

The rise in AI-generated queries comes at a time when residential conveyancing remains the most complained-about area of legal practice. According to data from the Legal Ombudsman, conveyancing complaints accounted for 36% of all accepted grievances in 2025/26, representing a 41% increase compared to the previous year. Common concerns included poor communication, delays, and failure to progress transactions.

Whilst buyers may use AI to feel more informed and in control, conveyancers caution that relying on these tools without proper oversight can lead to complications. Homebuyers might consider discussing their concerns directly with their conveyancer to ensure accurate and timely responses.

As technology continues to evolve, the property industry may need to adapt to new challenges posed by AI. For now, conveyancers are urging buyers to use these tools cautiously, recognising their limitations in complex legal processes.

item.title: Agents face rental stock squeeze as new landlord charge looms
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Letting agents across England may face dwindling rental stock as landlords grapple with new annual charges under the government's forthcoming rental property register. With fees set at £65 per occupied property, industry experts warn this additional cost could accelerate landlord exits from the private rental sector - potentially shrinking available housing for tenants and creating fresh challenges for agents.

Mounting Pressures on Landlords

The new registration scheme, beginning its phased rollout in the West Midlands this December before expanding nationally during 2027, adds to an increasingly complex landscape for property investors. While the individual £65 fee appears modest, professionals highlight how it compounds existing financial burdens including:

  • Rising mortgage costs following successive base rate increases
  • Ongoing tax changes affecting rental income
  • Expanding safety and maintenance obligations
  • Broader regulatory reforms in the private rented sector

For portfolio landlords, these costs multiply quickly - £325 annually for five properties or £650 for ten. Property experts suggest that while no single factor may trigger sales, the cumulative impact could prove decisive for landlords already considering exit strategies.

Potential Ripple Effects Across the Market

Current market conditions amplify concerns about reduced rental supply. Recent ONS data shows English private rents averaging £1,459 monthly, marking a 4% annual increase. Should landlords withdraw properties faster than new investment enters the market, two key consequences could emerge:

  • For letting agents: Increased competition for fewer landlord instructions, particularly in regions with high demand
  • For tenants: Intensified competition for available properties, potentially driving rents higher in constrained markets

The ultimate effect on housing availability hinges on who purchases properties sold by departing landlords. Sales to other investors maintain rental stock, while purchases by owner-occupiers permanently remove homes from the private rented sector.

Industry voices are calling for government monitoring of these trends, emphasising that policies designed to improve standards shouldn't unintentionally reduce housing access. As the registration scheme expands, its impact on market dynamics will become clearer - with letting agents, landlords and tenants all watching closely.

item.title: Prices rise as buyers return from summer break
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Recent data suggests that the UK property market is experiencing a resurgence in activity as buyers return from their summer break. Whilst this uptick in demand has led to a modest increase in property prices, experts caution that high stock levels and ongoing affordability challenges mean pricing remains a critical factor in securing successful sales.

Seasonal trends driving market activity

The property market often sees a seasonal boost in activity following the summer months, as potential buyers refocus their attention on moving plans. This year appears to be no exception, with estate agents reporting a noticeable increase in enquiries and viewings. However, whilst demand has picked up, the market remains competitive, with sellers needing to price their homes realistically to attract serious offers.

Mortgage rates, though still higher than in recent years, have stabilised slightly, which may be encouraging some buyers to re-enter the market. Nevertheless, affordability pressures persist, particularly for first-time buyers and those reliant on borrowing. As a result, sellers who price their properties too optimistically risk deterring interest in an environment where buyers are increasingly cautious.

Balancing supply and demand

One notable feature of the current market is the relatively high level of available stock. With more properties on the market compared to previous years, buyers have a greater choice, which can lead to longer decision-making processes and tougher negotiations. For sellers, this means that pricing competitively is more important than ever to stand out in a crowded marketplace.

Experts suggest that sellers who work closely with their estate agents to set realistic asking prices are more likely to achieve successful outcomes. Additionally, presenting a property in its best light and addressing any minor repairs or cosmetic improvements could help attract potential buyers.

The outlook for the coming months

As the market moves into the autumn and winter months, activity is expected to remain steady, though not necessarily at the levels seen in previous years. Economic factors such as inflation and interest rates will continue to influence buyer confidence, and affordability challenges are likely to persist. However, for those who are in a position to move, the current market conditions could present opportunities, particularly if sellers are willing to negotiate.

Borrowers might consider seeking advice from mortgage brokers to explore their options and secure competitive rates. With the right approach, both buyers and sellers could navigate the market effectively in the months ahead.

In summary, whilst the return of buyers from the summer break has injected some momentum into the property market, pricing remains a key factor in achieving successful sales. With high stock levels and affordability pressures shaping the landscape, sellers and buyers alike may benefit from a cautious and informed approach.

item.title: Newcastle tops property investor index
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Recent research has revealed that Newcastle has emerged as the top location for property investment in the UK. The city’s combination of strong rental yields, affordable property prices, and favourable market conditions has made it an attractive option for investors looking to expand their portfolios.

Why Newcastle Stands Out

Newcastle’s appeal lies in its balanced mix of affordability and potential returns. Property prices in the city remain relatively low compared to other major UK cities, making it accessible for investors with varying budgets. At the same time, rental demand is robust, driven by factors such as a growing student population and professionals seeking affordable housing options. This has resulted in competitive rental yields, which are a key consideration for many property investors.

Market Conditions and Future Prospects

The city’s property market has also benefited from ongoing regeneration projects and infrastructure improvements. These developments are enhancing Newcastle’s appeal as a place to live and work, which could further boost property values in the coming years. Additionally, the city’s strong local economy and employment opportunities contribute to its stability, providing a solid foundation for long-term investment.

For those considering property investment, Newcastle’s combination of affordability, rental potential, and positive market conditions makes it a compelling choice. However, as with any investment, thorough research and professional advice are essential to ensure informed decision-making.

item.title: Bridging finance key to below market property purchases
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

In the fast-paced world of property investment, securing a below-market-value deal can be a golden opportunity. However, acting swiftly is often essential to capitalise on such prospects. Bridging finance has emerged as a valuable tool for investors looking to move quickly and secure these discounted properties in a competitive market.

What is Bridging Finance?

Bridging finance is a short-term loan designed to "bridge" the gap between purchasing a property and securing long-term financing or selling an existing asset. Typically, these loans are used for a period of six months to two years, offering flexibility and speed that traditional mortgages may not provide. For property investors, this can be particularly advantageous when time is of the essence.

How Bridging Finance Facilitates Below-Market Purchases

Properties sold below market value often arise from situations where the seller needs a quick sale, such as probate, divorce, or financial distress. In such cases, investors who can act rapidly are more likely to secure these deals. Bridging finance enables buyers to complete purchases swiftly, often within days or weeks, giving them an edge over competitors relying on slower financing options.

Additionally, bridging loans can be tailored to suit specific needs, such as covering renovation costs or auction purchases. This versatility makes them a practical solution for investors aiming to maximise their returns on below-market-value properties.

Considerations for Using Bridging Finance

Whilst bridging finance offers significant benefits, borrowers might consider the following factors before proceeding:

  • Interest Rates: Bridging loans typically carry higher interest rates compared to traditional mortgages, so it’s important to factor in the cost.
  • Repayment Plan: Having a clear exit strategy, such as selling the property or refinancing, is crucial to avoid financial strain.
  • Lender Criteria: Different lenders have varying requirements, so investors should compare options to find the best fit for their circumstances.

For property investors seeking to capitalise on discounted opportunities, bridging finance could be a powerful tool. By enabling swift action and offering flexibility, it opens doors to below-market purchases that might otherwise be out of reach. However, careful planning and consideration of the associated costs are essential to ensure a successful investment.

item.title: Luxury London rents surge as supply dries up
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Luxury rental prices in prime central London have soared over the past year, according to recent research from Beauchamp Estates. Their Millionaires Letting in London survey reveals that average weekly rents for high-end houses and mansions surged by 67.2%, reaching £4,177 in the first half of 2026, up from £2,499 in 2025. Meanwhile, luxury apartments and penthouses saw a 15.1% increase, with average rents climbing to £1,957 per week. The findings highlight a growing disparity between supply and demand in the capital’s most exclusive rental market.

Supply Shortages Drive Price Hikes

The sharp rise in luxury rents coincides with a significant drop in the number of high-end lettings transactions. Beauchamp Estates recorded just 1,911 rentals above £1,000 per week in the first half of 2026, a 44.5% decline compared to the same period in 2025. This shortage of available properties has pushed prices upwards, particularly for the most expensive homes. Properties renting for over £3,000 per week now account for a larger share of the market, with those above £5,000 per week making up 5.23% of transactions, up from 4% in 2025.

Landlords’ increasing costs and regulatory changes have contributed to the shrinking supply. The introduction of the Renters’ Rights Act in May 2026, which abolished Section 21 evictions and shifted to assured periodic tenancies, has prompted some property owners to exit the market. Additionally, upcoming changes to property income tax rates, set to take effect from April 2027, have further discouraged investment in the rental sector.

Growing Demand from Wealthy Tenants

Whilst supply has dwindled, demand for luxury rentals remains robust. Beauchamp Estates reported a 30% increase in enquiries from Middle Eastern applicants, alongside a 20% rise from US tenants and a 5% uptick from Chinese renters. The agency noted that seven in ten ultra-prime households in London now opt to rent rather than buy, valuing the flexibility that renting offers. Many wealthy tenants choose to rent for periods of one to three years, aligning with their transient lifestyles.

The shift towards higher-value properties has also influenced the market’s revenue distribution. Homes renting for more than £5,000 per week generated £24.09 million in the first half of 2026, accounting for 22% of prime central London’s rental revenue, up from 18% the previous year.

As the luxury rental market continues to evolve, homeowners and investors may wish to monitor these trends closely. With supply constraints and strong demand showing no signs of easing, the dynamics of London’s high-end lettings market could remain volatile in the coming years.

item.title: Property industry reacts to latest Rightmove House Price Index
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

As the UK housing market enters its traditional autumn season, there are signs of renewed activity, with new seller asking prices rising for the first time since May. According to the latest Rightmove House Price Index, average asking prices increased by 0.7% in September, reaching £367,440. This uptick coincides with a seasonal boost in buyer interest following the summer slowdown. However, the market remains challenging, with the number of available homes hitting a 12-year high and buyer enquiries and agreed sales both down by 9% compared to last year. Rising mortgage rates, which have climbed from 5.09% to 5.29% for the average two-year fixed deal, are also adding pressure to both buyers and sellers.

Seller Optimism Meets Market Realities

Estate agents have noted a cautious sense of optimism among sellers, particularly as viewings have increased since the end of the summer holidays. However, experts emphasise that asking prices are not the same as selling prices. Jeremy Leaf, a north London estate agent and former RICS residential chairman, highlighted that asking prices often serve as an aspirational starting point rather than a definitive figure. He added that affordability concerns, driven by higher inflation and mortgage rates, are influencing buyer behaviour. Sellers who demonstrate flexibility in pricing are more likely to receive acceptable offers, though the pace of sales remains slow due to the abundance of available properties across most price ranges.

The Importance of Realistic Pricing

Kevin James, managing director at Bradleys Estate Agents, echoed these sentiments, noting that sellers who priced their homes realistically during the summer months experienced better-than-expected activity. With families returning from holidays and the new school year beginning, the market is seeing its traditional autumn uplift. However, James stressed that realistic pricing remains critical, particularly in regions like the South West, where there is greater choice for buyers. He also emphasised the importance of strong property presentation and advised sellers to adapt swiftly to market conditions to secure a sale.

Looking Beyond the Headlines

Ian Harris, president of NAEA Propertymark, cautioned buyers and sellers to look beyond the headline increase in asking prices. While the seasonal boost in activity is encouraging, buyer demand remains below last year’s levels, and affordability continues to be a key concern. Harris advised homeowners to carefully consider market conditions and seek professional advice to navigate the current landscape effectively.

As the housing market navigates this transitional period, sellers may wish to focus on realistic pricing and flexibility to attract buyers. Meanwhile, borrowers could benefit from exploring their mortgage options to secure deals that align with their financial circumstances. With the market showing signs of seasonal momentum, staying informed and adaptable will be key for those looking to move in the coming months.

item.title: Opinion: Forget the landlord exodus – this is service failure
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The UK lettings market has seen significant shifts in recent years, with many landlords opting to reduce their portfolios or exit the sector entirely. Whilst factors such as rising mortgage costs, taxation changes, and stricter regulations have contributed to this trend, experts suggest that a deeper issue lies in the quality of service provided by letting agents. According to industry professionals, landlords are not just leaving due to external pressures—many are departing because they haven’t been adequately supported to navigate the challenges of the modern property market.

Is It Really a Landlord Exodus?

The term "landlord exodus" has been widely used to describe the current trend, but this framing may oversimplify the situation. Recent data from the Government’s English Private Landlord Survey 2024 reveals that 31% of landlords plan to reduce their portfolios over the next two years, with 16% intending to sell all their properties. Only 7% aim to expand their holdings. However, this doesn’t necessarily mean landlords are abandoning the sector entirely. Many are simply reassessing their investments, restructuring their portfolios, or seeking better-performing properties.

Industry expert Sally Lawson highlights that whilst external pressures like the Renters’ Rights Act and rising costs are real, they are not the sole reasons for landlords’ decisions. Instead, she argues that a lack of tailored support from letting agencies has played a significant role. Without guidance on how to stay profitable, reduce risk, or plan a structured exit, many landlords feel left to navigate these challenges alone. This suggests that the issue is as much about service failure as it is about market conditions.

The Role of Letting Agents in Retaining Landlords

Despite the challenges, some letting agencies have managed to grow their managed stock significantly. For example, one branch of Concentric Lettings reportedly increased its portfolio by over 25% organically, even as other agencies experienced losses. This demonstrates that there is still potential for growth in the sector, but it requires a proactive and personalised approach to landlord support.

Many landlords are facing a range of pressures, from refinancing costs and rising repair bills to poor returns on equity. Others are nearing retirement and require help to develop a structured exit plan. Yet, too often, letting agencies treat all landlords the same, offering generic newsletters and standard management packages. This one-size-fits-all approach is no longer sufficient in a market that demands tailored solutions.

Landlords who receive personalised advice on portfolio restructuring, risk mitigation, or strategic exits are more likely to remain in the sector. Those who feel unsupported, however, may choose to sell or self-manage their properties. This highlights the importance of letting agencies evolving their services to meet the diverse needs of today’s landlords.

A Growing Need for Innovation in the Lettings Market

As the lettings market continues to evolve, letting agencies must adapt to retain their clients. This could involve offering more flexible management packages, providing expert advice on portfolio optimisation, or helping landlords identify higher-performing investments. By addressing the specific concerns of landlords—whether they’re dealing with rising costs, regulatory changes, or retirement planning—agents can play a crucial role in shaping the future of the sector.

Ultimately, whilst external factors like legislation and market conditions will always influence landlord decisions, the quality of service provided by letting agencies remains a key factor in determining their next steps. Agencies that innovate and offer tailored support may find themselves better positioned to thrive in an increasingly competitive market.

item.title: Landlord exodus hits record high – but rental stock rises
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

The UK’s private rental sector is experiencing a significant shift, with landlords exiting the market at a record rate whilst rental stock continues to grow. According to data from TwentyEA, an average of 562 properties have left the sector each day during the third quarter of this year, totalling around 44,000 properties. This marks a notable increase compared to 495 daily exits at the same time last year and a stark contrast to the 167 daily average seen at the start of the decade. Despite this trend, the overall availability of rental properties has risen by 1.3% over the past year, painting a complex picture for letting agents and renters alike.

Rising Stock Amid Landlord Exits

While the number of landlords leaving the market has surged, the volume of rental properties available has increased. This growth is partly driven by a higher number of new properties entering the market compared to the number of lets agreed. Additionally, the rise in build-to-rent developments has contributed to the expansion of rental stock. This comes after several years of declining availability, offering some relief to renters in certain price brackets.

However, the situation varies significantly depending on the rental price range. Properties priced between £800 and £1,500 per month have seen a 7% year-on-year increase in availability. In contrast, the supply of homes priced between £1,500 and £3,000 has fallen by 1.1%, whilst properties above £3,000 have experienced a more substantial decline of 6.5%. Regionally, ten out of thirteen areas analysed showed an increase in stock, with Wales leading the way at a 15.2% rise. Meanwhile, Yorkshire and Inner London both saw a 5.3% drop in available properties.

Growth in New Rental Supply

The flow of new properties onto the rental market has also seen a sharp increase. Data reveals that 118,100 more properties have entered the market this year compared to the same period in 2025, representing a 13.6% rise—the highest level in seven years. This growth has been observed across all rental price brackets, with the strongest increases seen in properties priced below £1,500. New supply for homes under £800 rose by 14.5%, whilst the £800 to £1,500 bracket saw a 16% increase.

Regionally, every area except Northern Ireland recorded an increase in new rental supply. Wales once again topped the list with a 26.8% surge, whilst Inner London saw the smallest rise at 8.8%. This influx of new properties has helped balance the market, particularly in more affordable segments.

Rental Activity and Rent Trends

Rental activity has also strengthened, albeit at a slower pace than the growth in supply. The number of lets agreed has increased by 3.3% compared to 2025, reaching the highest level in seven years. Properties priced below £800 per month saw a 5.4% rise in agreed lets, whilst the £800 to £1,500 bracket recorded a 5.2% increase. Wales experienced the strongest regional growth, with lets agreed up by 12.3%, while Inner London saw a 2% decline.

Despite these changes in supply and demand, average agreed rents have remained broadly flat. This suggests that the increased availability of properties, particularly in lower price brackets, is helping to stabilise rental costs for many tenants.

The UK rental market is undergoing a period of transformation, with landlord exits, rising stock, and varying trends across price brackets and regions. Whilst the overall picture remains complex, the increase in available properties offers potential opportunities for renters navigating the market.

item.title: Conveyancer numbers plunge as sales take 123 days to exchange
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

The UK’s residential conveyancing sector is facing mounting pressure as solicitor numbers decline whilst property sales take an average of 123 days to reach exchange. According to recent industry reports, these challenges could create bottlenecks in housing transactions, leaving estate agents and homeowners navigating extended waiting periods.

Declining conveyancer numbers raise concerns

Recent data from the IRN UK Residential Conveyancing Market Report reveals there were 10,724 solicitors specialising in residential property transactions across England and Wales in January 2026. This marks a significant reduction of over 2,000 practitioners compared to 2021 figures. The report also indicates that just 5,904 law firms remain active in residential conveyancing, highlighting a notable contraction in sector capacity.

This shrinking professional pool coincides with increasingly complex regulatory requirements. Since April 2025, conveyancers have faced stricter anti-money laundering rules alongside new TA6 and TA7 property forms and revised regulations. These added compliance burdens may be contributing to the profession’s declining numbers whilst simultaneously increasing workloads for remaining practitioners.

Lengthy transaction times strain the market

Separate analysis from TwentyCi shows the average property sale now takes approximately 123 days to reach exchange, with considerable regional variations. Such protracted timelines increase the risk of transaction chains collapsing and leave estate agents managing sales for extended periods before completion.

Access Legal’s State of the UK Conveyancing Market report reinforces these concerns, examining 15 months of HM Land Registry data from April 2025 to June 2026. The research suggests conveyancing firms are grappling with growing workloads amid shrinking resources, potentially creating further delays in property transactions.

Andrew Stevens of Access Legal commented: “Law firms can’t simply ask conveyancers to work longer hours to solve the deficit challenge.” He suggests technological solutions could help alleviate some pressure, noting: “While the likes of technology and AI cannot replace empathy or judgement, they can help in alleviating stress and ultimately contribute to preventing burnout.”

Homeowners and buyers navigating the current market may wish to factor in these extended timelines when planning property moves. With conveyancing capacity under strain, seeking recommendations for responsive legal professionals and allowing generous timeframes could help smooth the transaction process.

item.title: Rolling contracts now dominate the private rented sector
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The UK's private rental sector has seen a dramatic shift towards rolling tenancy agreements, with new research revealing that four in five landlords now exclusively use these flexible arrangements. Data from property platform Lendlord indicates that 79% of surveyed landlords currently operate on periodic tenancies, while fewer than 15% maintain fixed-term contracts.

The rapid rise of rolling contracts

Industry experts have observed a striking acceleration in the adoption of rolling tenancies since legislative changes came into force earlier this year. The Renters' Rights Act, which took effect on 1st May, automatically transferred assured tenancies onto periodic systems in England. Lendlord's analysis of over 15,000 tenancies shows this transition occurred remarkably quickly – where 31.3% of tenancies starting in October 2025 were fixed-term, this figure had collapsed to just 0.9% by August 2026.

The research suggests landlords are embracing the flexibility of rolling contracts, which automatically renew on a weekly or monthly basis unless terminated by either party. This move away from traditional fixed-term agreements reflects a broader trend towards more adaptable tenancy structures in the post-reform rental market.

Letting agents' crucial role in documentation

With the shift to periodic tenancies, attention has turned to the quality and clarity of tenancy agreements. The study found that 45% of landlords obtained their latest agreements directly from letting agents, yet nearly 90% admitted these documents hadn't undergone solicitor review. This gap highlights agents' growing responsibility in ensuring contracts comply with new regulations.

Interestingly, a quarter of surveyed landlords stated that professional legal review would increase their confidence in tenancy paperwork – the most common response. This suggests many property owners feel uncertain about their current agreement's robustness, despite the widespread adoption of rolling contracts.

  • 79% of landlords now use rolling tenancies exclusively
  • Just 14.5% maintain fixed-term only portfolios
  • 90% of agreements haven't had legal review
  • 25% of landlords want solicitor-checked paperwork

Property professionals emphasise that while adopting periodic tenancies is an important first step, landlords must also ensure their documentation clearly outlines obligations under the new regime. As the rental landscape continues evolving, both landlords and agents may wish to review their processes to maintain compliance and protect all parties' interests.

item.title: Improvement notices and the consequences of non-compliance
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Local authorities have the power to issue improvement notices when rental properties fail to meet required standards, and landlords who ignore these warnings could face substantial penalties. Understanding the process and potential consequences is crucial for property owners who want to avoid costly enforcement action under the Housing Act 2004.

How improvement notices work

When council inspectors identify hazards or maintenance issues in a rental property, they may serve an improvement notice outlining necessary repairs within a specified timeframe. Common issues include:

  • Damp or mould problems
  • Structural defects
  • Faulty electrical systems
  • Inadequate fire safety measures

Landlords who fail to complete the required works by the deadline commit an offence, with local authorities able to prosecute or impose civil penalties. From May 2026, the maximum financial penalty rises to £40,000, with £25,000 as the recommended starting point for serious breaches.

The appeal process and recent legal clarification

A recent Court of Appeal case (Manaquel Company Ltd v London Borough of Lambeth) has clarified important aspects of improvement notice enforcement. The court ruled that authorities must assess property conditions at the time the notice was served, not when any subsequent appeal is heard.

This means that while landlords may complete repairs after receiving a notice, this doesn't automatically invalidate the original enforcement action if the property was substandard when inspected. Evidence of later improvements can only be considered if it helps establish the property's condition at the time of the initial inspection.

Consequences of non-compliance

Once works are completed, local authorities must revoke the improvement notice under Section 16(1) of the Housing Act 2004. However, any financial penalties already imposed for late compliance typically remain payable. Landlords should be aware that:

  • Penalties are separate from the cost of remedial works
  • Payment deadlines are usually strict with limited appeal options
  • Multiple offences can lead to escalating penalties

Property owners who receive an improvement notice may wish to seek professional advice promptly, both to address the immediate issues and to understand their legal position regarding any potential penalties. Keeping detailed records of all communications and repair works could prove valuable if disputes arise.

With stricter enforcement and higher fines coming into effect, maintaining properties to the required standards has never been more important for landlords. Regular inspections and prompt attention to maintenance issues remain the best approach to avoiding enforcement action.

item.title: The new deposit trap for Section 8 possession claims
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Landlords navigating possession claims under Section 8 should be aware of recent legislative changes affecting deposit protection requirements. The Renters Rights Act 2025 has amended Section 215 of the Housing Act 2004, creating new considerations for property owners seeking possession orders when deposits haven't been properly safeguarded.

Deposit protection rules clarified

Since April 2007, landlords have been legally required to protect tenants' deposits in government-approved schemes. While many still fail to comply, the consequences have evolved following the abolition of Section 21 'no-fault' evictions. The amended legislation now stipulates that courts may only grant possession orders if:

  • The deposit is held in an authorised scheme
  • All relevant scheme requirements have been met
  • Prescribed information has been properly served to tenants

Notably, the strict 30-day protection deadline has been relaxed - landlords can still obtain possession orders if they protect deposits before the court hearing.

Implications for Section 8 claims

The changes affect nearly all Section 8 possession grounds, with two key exceptions. Ground 7A (serious anti-social behaviour) and Ground 14 (nuisance or criminal activity) remain unaffected by deposit protection status. For all other grounds, landlords must demonstrate compliance with deposit rules before a possession order can be granted.

This means that whilst landlords can still issue Section 8 notices and begin proceedings without protected deposits, their claims will ultimately fail unless they either protect the deposit before the hearing date or return the deposit (either in full or with agreed deductions).

Options for non-compliant landlords

Property owners who haven't protected deposits might consider several approaches:

  • Protecting the deposit immediately and serving prescribed information, noting that some schemes have specific late protection rules
  • Returning the deposit, either in full or with tenant-approved deductions
  • Resolving any existing tenant claims regarding unprotected deposits

With Section 21 no longer available, maintaining full compliance with deposit protection regulations has become even more crucial for landlords seeking possession through Section 8. Whilst late protection is now permitted for possession purposes, landlords should be aware that tenants may still pursue separate claims for compensation regarding initially unprotected deposits.

The changes highlight the importance of proper deposit handling from the outset of a tenancy. Landlords may wish to review their processes to ensure full compliance with current legislation, particularly when considering possession actions.

item.title: Rent guarantor demand surges as landlords adapt to Renters’ Rights Act
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The rental market has seen a dramatic 50% surge in demand for rent guarantors since the introduction of the Renters’ Rights Act, according to new data from specialist provider Housing Hand. The figures highlight how landlords and letting agents are adjusting their tenant vetting processes following the regulatory changes that came into force on 1 May.

Why guarantors are becoming more important

Under the new legislation, landlords can no longer request more than one month’s rent in advance from tenants. This restriction has led many property owners to seek alternative financial safeguards, with guarantor agreements emerging as a popular solution. These legally binding contracts allow a third party – typically a family member – to cover rental payments if the tenant defaults.

Graham Hayward of Housing Hand explained: “With the cap on advance rent payments, many landlords now view guarantors as an essential part of their risk management strategy.” The company’s data shows this shift has occurred despite no significant increase in actual claims against guarantor agreements, with annual payouts remaining stable at around £1.5 million.

Changing tenant referencing practices

The regulatory changes appear to be prompting a broader transformation in tenant screening processes. Alongside the rise in guarantor requests, Housing Hand has observed growing demand for enhanced background checks, including:

  • Sanctions screening
  • Politically exposed person (PEP) checks
  • Detailed income verification

These developments suggest the rental market is becoming more regulated, with landlords placing greater emphasis on financial security measures. While the legislation aims to make renting more accessible, the increased focus on guarantors could potentially create barriers for tenants without access to suitable guarantors.

For those struggling to find a guarantor, specialist providers offer commercial guarantor services, though these typically come at a cost. Prospective tenants might wish to factor these potential expenses into their budgeting when planning a rental application.

The Housing Hand data provides valuable early insights into how the rental sector is adapting to the new regulatory environment. As the market continues to evolve, both landlords and tenants may need to stay informed about these changing dynamics.

item.title: Landlord Law Newsround #454
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The government is facing questions over how it plans to share landlord data between the new Private Rented Sector (PRS) Database and the Landlord Ombudsman. Housing Minister Matthew Pennycook has acknowledged that details on the process remain unclear. Whilst the Ombudsman will share information about non-compliant landlords with local authorities, it is not yet known how much of this data tenants will be able to access. Concerns have been raised about privacy, as many landlords are private individuals who may not wish to have their information made public, yet will be required to register. Sean Hooker of the Property Redress Scheme has urged caution, noting that neither property agents nor private landlords currently have a regulator. He emphasised that the database will not serve as a regulatory or enforcement body.

Landlords Becoming More Cautious in Tenant Selection

Recent statistics suggest that landlords are taking extra precautions when selecting tenants, driven by concerns over the eviction process following the introduction of the Renters’ Rights Act. According to a survey by The Lettings Hub, 95% of letting agents lack confidence in the court system, particularly regarding the time it takes to evict tenants. Beth Richardson, Head of Operations at The Lettings Hub, has warned that excessive caution could reduce the supply of rental properties. She recommends that landlords thoroughly reference tenants and consider using professional guarantors. Additionally, she highlights the importance of practical guidance on the new possession process to help landlords navigate these changes effectively.

EPC Reforms to Consider Property Characteristics

Energy Minister Martin McCluskey has announced that the upcoming Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) reforms will take into account the unique characteristics of each property. An enhanced exemption regime has been drafted, ensuring that any energy improvements made before 2030 to achieve an EPC C rating by 1 October 2029 will remain compliant until the certificate expires or is replaced. The government has also set a maximum expenditure threshold for these improvements, recognising the need for energy efficiency measures to be sensitive to the property’s individual features.

As the private rented sector continues to evolve, landlords and tenants alike are navigating a landscape of new regulations and reforms. Staying informed about these changes could help both parties adapt to the shifting requirements and expectations in the housing market.
